These notes derive the estimating equation in [Lecture 6.2](../lectures/lecture6.2.qmd){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} one step at a time. They start from the utility function on the Model slide and end at the equation on the estimation slides. The notation follows @nevo2000practitioner.

## Step 1: the utility function

Consumer $i$ in market $t$ gets this utility from product $j$:

$$
u_{ijt} = \alpha_i(y_i - p_{jt}) + x_{jt}\beta_i + \xi_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}
$$

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $y_i$ | Income of consumer $i$ |
| $p_{jt}$ | Price of product $j$ in market $t$ |
| $\alpha_i$ | Marginal utility of income for consumer $i$ |
| $x_{jt}$ | Characteristics the researcher observes, such as sugar content |
| $\beta_i$ | Consumer $i$'s tastes for those characteristics |
| $\xi_{jt}$ | Characteristics the researcher does not observe, such as brand quality or promotions |
| $\varepsilon_{ijt}$ | A shock specific to this consumer and product |

Economists call this a conditional indirect utility: the highest utility the consumer can reach, given that the consumer buys product $j$.

## Step 2: why income minus price

The term $y_i - p_{jt}$ is the money the consumer has left after buying product $j$. That money buys everything else, and each dollar of it is worth $\alpha_i$ units of utility. The term $\alpha_i(y_i - p_{jt})$ is therefore the utility from everything else the consumer can still afford.

Expanding the term shows the two parts:

$$
\alpha_i(y_i - p_{jt}) = \alpha_i y_i - \alpha_i p_{jt}
$$

The second part is why a higher price lowers utility. @nevo2000practitioner notes that this form comes from a quasilinear utility function, which has no wealth effects. He calls that reasonable for cereal and unreasonable for cars, and BLP use $\log(y_i - p_{jt})$ for that reason.

## Step 3: the outside good

A consumer can also buy none of the products. This is the outside good, labeled $j = 0$. After the standard normalization, the consumer keeps all income:

$$
u_{i0t} = \alpha_i y_i + \varepsilon_{i0t}
$$

## Step 4: where income goes

A consumer picks the option with the highest utility, so only differences in utility across options affect the choice. The term $\alpha_i y_i$ is the same in every option, including the outside good, so it cancels from every difference:

$$
u_{ijt} - u_{i0t} = -\alpha_i p_{jt} + x_{jt}\beta_i + \xi_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt} - \varepsilon_{i0t}
$$

Income leaves the choice problem as a level. It can still matter through tastes: in the full model, $\alpha_i$ can vary with income, so higher-income consumers can be less sensitive to price. Dropping $\alpha_i y_i$ gives the equivalent form:

$$
u_{ijt} = -\alpha_i p_{jt} + x_{jt}\beta_i + \xi_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}, \qquad u_{i0t} = \varepsilon_{i0t}
$$

## Step 5: the logit case

The logit model assumes every consumer has the same tastes, so $\alpha_i = \alpha$ and $\beta_i = \beta$. All differences between consumers then come from $\varepsilon_{ijt}$.

Collect everything that is common to all consumers into the mean utility $\delta_{jt}$:

$$
\delta_{jt} = x_{jt}\beta - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt}
$$

Utility becomes $u_{ijt} = \delta_{jt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}$. The outside good has $\delta_{0t} = 0$.

## Step 6: from utility to market shares

The researcher does not see $\varepsilon_{ijt}$, so the model predicts the probability that a consumer picks each option. With many consumers, that probability is the product's market share.

The logit model assumes $\varepsilon_{ijt}$ is independent across products and consumers and follows a Type I extreme value distribution. This assumption gives a closed-form share [@nevo2000practitioner, equation 6]:

$$
s_{jt} = \frac{\exp(\delta_{jt})}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{J} \exp(\delta_{kt})}, \qquad s_{0t} = \frac{1}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{J} \exp(\delta_{kt})}
$$

The 1 in each denominator is $\exp(0)$, the outside good.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional: where the share formula comes from

Drop the market subscript and let $A = \sum_{k=0}^{J} \exp(\delta_k)$, which includes the outside good. The Type I extreme value distribution has CDF $F(\varepsilon) = \exp(-e^{-\varepsilon})$ and density $f(\varepsilon) = e^{-\varepsilon}\exp(-e^{-\varepsilon})$.

Product $j$ is chosen when $\delta_j + \varepsilon_j \geq \delta_k + \varepsilon_k$ for every other option $k$. Given $\varepsilon_j = \varepsilon$, this has probability

$$
\prod_{k \neq j} F(\varepsilon + \delta_j - \delta_k)
$$

Averaging over $\varepsilon$ and combining the exponents gives

$$
s_j = \int e^{-\varepsilon} \exp\left(-e^{-\varepsilon} e^{-\delta_j} A\right) d\varepsilon
$$

Substitute $w = e^{-\varepsilon}$, so $dw = -e^{-\varepsilon} d\varepsilon$ and $w$ runs from 0 to $\infty$:

$$
s_j = \int_0^\infty \exp\left(-w\, e^{-\delta_j} A\right) dw = \frac{e^{\delta_j}}{A}
$$
:::

## Step 7: take logs

The two shares have the same denominator, so dividing cancels it:

$$
\frac{s_{jt}}{s_{0t}} = \exp(\delta_{jt})
$$

Taking logs gives the inversion in @berry1994estimating:

$$
\ln s_{jt} - \ln s_{0t} = \delta_{jt}
$$

Replacing $\delta_{jt}$ with its definition from Step 5 gives the estimating equation:

$$
\ln s_{jt} - \ln s_{0t} = x_{jt}\beta - \alpha p_{jt} + \xi_{jt}
$$

The left side comes from data on shares. The right side has data on characteristics and prices, parameters to estimate, and $\xi_{jt}$ as the error term. It is a linear regression.

**A numeric check.** Suppose product 1 has a 20 percent share, product 2 has a 30 percent share, and the outside good has 50 percent. Then $\delta_1 = \ln(0.2/0.5) = -0.92$ and $\delta_2 = \ln(0.3/0.5) = -0.51$. Going back through the share formula, $\exp(\delta_1) = 0.4$ and $\exp(\delta_2) = 0.6$, so the denominator is $1 + 0.4 + 0.6 = 2$. The shares are $0.4/2 = 0.2$ and $0.6/2 = 0.3$, which match.

## Step 8: why the regression needs instruments

Firms know $\xi_{jt}$ when they set prices, so $p_{jt}$ and $\xi_{jt}$ are correlated. Price is an endogenous regressor in the equation above, and OLS gives a biased estimate of $\alpha$. Instruments that shift price and are uncorrelated with $\xi_{jt}$ solve this problem, as in any linear instrumental-variables regression.

A reported coefficient on price of $-30.05$ means $\alpha = 30.05$.

## Step 9: random coefficients

The random-coefficients logit returns to tastes that vary. Each consumer's tastes depend on demographics $D_i$ and on unobserved traits $v_i$ [@nevo2000practitioner, equation 2]:

$$
\begin{pmatrix} \alpha_i \\ \beta_i \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha \\ \beta \end{pmatrix} + \Pi D_i + \Sigma v_i
$$

The mean tastes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ stay in $\delta_{jt}$. The deviation from the mean moves into a consumer-specific term $\mu_{ijt}$:

$$
u_{ijt} = \delta_{jt} + \mu_{ijt} + \varepsilon_{ijt}
$$

Conditional on a consumer's tastes, Step 6 still applies. Market shares are the average of those logit probabilities across consumers:

$$
s_{jt} = \int \frac{\exp(\delta_{jt} + \mu_{ijt})}{1 + \sum_{k=1}^{J} \exp(\delta_{kt} + \mu_{ikt})}\, dP(D, v)
$$

This integral has no closed form, so the division in Step 7 no longer works. The software approximates it by averaging over a set of simulated consumers, and it finds $\delta_{jt}$ numerically. The logic of the inversion is unchanged: find the mean utilities that make predicted shares equal observed shares.

## Step 10: the estimation loop

For a guess of the parameters in $\Pi$ and $\Sigma$:

1. Compute predicted shares by averaging over simulated consumers.
2. Find the $\delta_{jt}$ that make predicted shares equal observed shares. BLP's contraction mapping updates each mean utility by the log difference between observed and predicted shares until they match [@nevo2000practitioner, equation 12]:

$$
\delta_{jt}^{h+1} = \delta_{jt}^{h} + \ln S_{jt} - \ln s_{jt}(\delta^{h})
$$

3. Run the linear instrumental-variables regression of $\delta_{jt}$ on price and characteristics. The residual is $\xi_{jt}$.
4. Compute the GMM objective, which measures how far $\xi_{jt}$ is from being uncorrelated with the instruments.
5. Update the guess and repeat until the objective reaches a minimum.

The logit model is the special case with $\Pi = 0$ and $\Sigma = 0$, where this loop collapses to the single regression in Step 7.

## Step 11: elasticities from the shares

Differentiating the logit share in Step 6 gives the price responses:

$$
\frac{\partial s_{jt}}{\partial p_{jt}} = -\alpha s_{jt}(1 - s_{jt}), \qquad \frac{\partial s_{jt}}{\partial p_{kt}} = \alpha s_{jt} s_{kt}
$$

Converting to elasticities gives [@nevo2000practitioner, page 522]:

$$
\eta_{jjt} = -\alpha p_{jt}(1 - s_{jt}), \qquad \eta_{jkt} = \alpha p_{kt} s_{kt}
$$

The cross-price elasticity $\eta_{jkt}$ has no $j$ in it. A rise in the price of $k$ moves every rival's share by the same percentage, which is the substitution restriction in the lecture. Random coefficients remove it, because each consumer has a separate $\alpha_i$ and separate choice probabilities [@nevo2000practitioner, page 525]:

$$
\eta_{jkt} = \frac{p_{kt}}{s_{jt}} \int \alpha_i\, s_{ijt}\, s_{ikt}\, dP(D, v) \quad \text{for } j \neq k
$$

Two products bought by the same consumers have probabilities $s_{ijt}$ and $s_{ikt}$ that are large together, which raises their cross-price elasticity. The [cereal demand demo](cereal-demand-demo.qmd){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} computes these quantities.
